First, a comet traverses the heavens; second, two suns appear simultaneously; third, the sun and moon undergo eclipses; fourth, rainbows portend misfortune; fifth, the five planets lose their regular courses; sixth, the great earth quakes; seventh, wells emit strange sounds; eighth, wind and rain deviate from their proper seasons; ninth, crops fail to ripen; tenth, enemies invade from other regions; eleventh, one's own country is not at peace.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!

When we, the four kings, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas and the long-standing benevolent spirits who protect the land depart, there will arise such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of calamities, portents, and evil events.”
[The] Binding. Sūtra: “World-Honored One!

If there is a king who wishes to protect his realm and constantly enjoy happiness; who wishes to cause all sentient beings to receive peace and security; who wishes to subdue all external enemies and ensure that his own kingdom remains forever prosperous; and who wishes to cause the True Teaching to spread throughout the world so that suffering and evil dharmas are all extinguished—World-Honored One!”
These kings will surely listen to and accept this wondrous King of Sutras, and they should likewise honor, make offerings to, read, recite, and uphold those who do so.

Through the power of these roots of goodness from hearing the Dharma, we and the immeasurable hosts of devas shall partake of the flavor of the unsurpassed nectar of the Dharma; our entire retinues and all other celestial beings shall likewise attain supreme benefit.
"For what reason?
Because this king of men has listened to and received this sutra with a sincere heart. Commentary:
The following section clarifies the benefits of propagation and protection, which consists of three parts:
first, the king’s formulation of virtuous vows;
second, from the passage "World-Honored One, these kings... onwards, the instruction to propagate the sutra.
Third, regarding the section beginning with "We and others," there are three parts concerning the benefits received by the Four Great Kings:
first, the heading; second, the interrogative inquiry "For what reason?"; and third, the subsequent explanation beginning with "Because this king of men... and so forth.
The heading states, "By means of this listening to the Dharma," and so forth; this is because the human king listens to the Dharma.
The section beginning with "We" clarifies how we, the Four Heavenly Kings and others, have obtained benefit.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!

Just as Mahābrahmā constantly proclaims both mundane and supramundane treatises for all sentient beings, and Śakra likewise expounds various treatises, and the ṛṣis with the five supernatural powers also expound various treatises.”
World-Honored One!

Although Brahmā, Śakra, and the seers with five supernatural powers possess hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of immeasurable treatises, yet because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity for the multitudes of devas and humans, has preached this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra, it surpasses all those previously mentioned by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of times, beyond any possible comparison.

Why is this? Because by means of this, all kings throughout Jambudvīpa may transform the world through the True Dharma (*saddharma*), bringing about matters that grant peace and happiness to sentient beings; protecting themselves and their retinues so they are free from suffering and affliction; ensuring they are not harmed by enemies or bandits from other regions; causing all evils to depart far away; and further eliminating calamities and misfortunes within their kingdoms, transforming them through the True Dharma so that there is no dispute or litigation.
"Therefore, O Kings of Men, each within your respective realms should naturally uphold the torch of Dharma, illuminating boundlessly and increasing the hosts of devas along with their retinues.
This concludes the third section, which measures and clarifies the excellence [of this teaching] and exhorts its propagation; it consists of three parts:
first, measuring and clarifying the excellence; second, the benefits conferred by the Four Heavenly Kings; and third, the exhortation to propagate the sutra.
The beginning consists of four parts:

first, the presentation of the inferior; second, from "The World-Honored One and Brahmā" onwards, the clarification of the superior; third, from "Why is this? onwards, the explanation of the reason; and fourth, from "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion regarding the upholding of the sutra.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!

We—the four kings, the immeasurable hosts of devas and yakṣas, and all the devas within Jambudvīpa—by means of these causes and conditions, shall partake of the flavor of the unsurpassed nectar of the Dharma; we shall obtain great majesty, power, and radiance, being fully endowed with them, and all sentient beings shall attain peace and security.”

Furthermore, in future ages, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of inconceivable nayutas of kalpas, they shall constantly experience happiness; thereafter, meeting immeasurable Buddhas and planting various roots of goodness, they will finally realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Such immeasurable and boundless benefits as these all arise because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through his great compassion surpasses the hosts of Brahmā; through his great wisdom exceeds Śakra; and through his cultivation of various ascetic practices excels the seers of the five supernatural powers by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of times beyond measure, as he expounds such a subtle and wondrous sūtra for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding the benefits for those below [the heavens], there are two parts:
first, the benefits for the devas; second, from "causing Jambudvīpa" onwards, the benefits for humans are clarified.
Within the benefits for the devas, there is first the attainment of benefit, followed by the praise beginning with "all these are the Tathāgata."

Sūtra: “May all the sovereigns of the nations in Jambudvīpa and all the multitudes of people clearly understand all worldly customs, as well as the matters of governing the state and transforming the people through exhortation. By the power of the circulation of this King of Sūtras, may they everywhere attain peace and happiness. All such benefits and blessings are due to the Great Teacher Śākyamuni’s extensive promotion of this scripture and his power of compassion.”
The following section concludes the benefits for persons.
Within this, only the benefit of attaining the cause is clarified, while its fruit is not mentioned because it was already explained previously.
First, the benefit of attaining the cause; second, the conclusion based on the sūtra.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!
For these reasons, all kings of men and others should uphold, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this wondrous king of sūtras.”
Why is this? Because such inconceivable, supreme merits and benefits are bestowed upon all; therefore, it is named the "Supreme King of Sutras.
Following this, there are three sections on the exhortation to propagate the sutra:
The headings, the indicators, and the detailed explanations are as follows.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:

"You, the Four Kings, along with your retinues—the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of celestial multitudes—if you see that a king of men is able to listen to this sūtra with a sincere heart, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising it, you should protect him, eliminate his misfortunes and afflictions, and enable you yourselves as well to receive peace and happiness."
Commentary: The second major section concerns the Four Kings’ vow to protect [the teachings] in accordance with the instructions.
This contains two parts:
First is protection of the body, followed by protection of the Dharma.
Above, the protection of the body was clarified; here below, the protection of the Dharma is clarified.
Previously, it was explained that the protection of the body protects both those who propagate the Dharma and the nation; here, it concerns only the protection of those who propagate the Dharma.
Furthermore, guarding the body eliminates all decline, calamity, pestilence, and every form of insecurity;
it removes poverty and suffering and causes one to obtain wealth. Therefore, the Buddha praised it, saying:
"You are able to tear asunder the net of poverty and suffering for all sentient beings, causing them to attain merit and happiness."
Having attained merit and happiness, one is then able to propagate the sutra; therefore, it is said next:
"Also cause this sutra to circulate widely in the world.
Within this, there are three parts:

First, the World-Honored One’s earnest exhortation; second, the Dharma-protection of the Four Heavenly Kings; and finally, from "At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa spoke this mantra" onwards, the World-Honored One’s praise.
This first section has two parts:
first, the exhortation to protect the human king, and second, the exhortation to protect the fourfold assembly.
This protection for the king of men consists of four parts within the text:

first, the command to the assembly of the Four Kings; second, those who are to be protected; third, the actual injunction to provide protection; and fourth, from the words "you shall be able to... onwards, the clarification of the reason why they must provide protection.

Sūtra: “If the fourfold assembly is able to widely disseminate this king of sūtras, they will extensively perform the work of a Buddha among humans and devas, universally benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.”

O Four Kings, you must always protect such persons and these four assemblies, preventing other external conditions from causing them interference or disturbance. You should cause their bodies and minds to be tranquil and at ease, so that this King of Sutras may be widely proclaimed and disseminated without interruption, benefiting sentient beings until the end of the future.
The exhortation to protect the fourfold assembly consists of four parts:

first, those who are to be protected; second, the praise of their efficacy beginning with "Among humans and devas"; third, the formal command to provide protection beginning with "Such persons as these"; and fourth, the clarification of the intent behind the protection beginning with "Regarding this sutra."
Sūtra. At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! I possess a dhāraṇī method of the wish-fulfilling jewel. If there are sentient beings who delight in receiving and upholding it, their merit will be immeasurable; I shall constantly protect them, causing those beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, and enabling them to accomplish the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.”
The Commentary states: The second section, "The Four Kings Protecting by Dharma," is divided into four parts:

first, the indication of the efficacy of the mantra; second, from "One who wishes to uphold... onwards, the two methods for upholding the mantra; third, from "At that time there was a Vaiśravaṇa... onwards, the clarification of the benefits obtained through the mantra; and fourth, from "Even if the sun and moon... onwards, the establishment of the vow to provide protection.
The initial text has three parts:
first, the person who recites the mantra; second, the title of the mantra; and third, from "If there are sentient beings... onwards, the efficacy of the mantra. The Sūtra says:
"Those who wish to receive and uphold [this teaching] should first recite this mantra for protecting the body."
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

“Namo vīśramaṇāya mahārājāya | Tadyathā | ra ra ra ra | kuṇu kuṇu | kūṇu kūṇu | kṣuṇu kṣuṇu | sava sava | kara kara | mahāvikarman | mahāvikarman | mahārāja hulu hulu | [insert one’s own name here] sarvasattvānām svāhā. [The two syllables *svā* and *hā* are both to be drawn out with a long tone. “World-Honored One!”
One who recites this mantra should consecrate a white thread with it seven times, tying a knot for each repetition, and fasten it behind the elbow; thus the matter will surely be accomplished.

One should take various incenses—namely, agallochum, sandalwood, camphor, storax, tagara, and frankincense—and blend them all in equal proportions. Holding an incense burner, one should burn the incense as an offering, bathe until pure, and wear fresh, clean garments; then, within a quiet room, one may recite the divine mantra.
The following clarifies the ritual procedure for maintaining the mantra.
There are three parts to this procedure:
first, the instruction on protecting the body; second, the instruction on invoking protection; and third, the actual instruction on the root mantra.
The initial instruction for protecting the body has three parts:
first, the designation of the mantra’s name; second, the actual recitation; and third, the World-Honored One’s recitation.
From the words “This mantra” onwards is the instruction on the ritual procedure for recitation.
Vaiśravaṇa means "Much-Hearing" (Bahuśruta); Mahā means "Great"; Rāja means "King"—the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
As for "Tagara," it means "Fragrant Incense."
Sūtra: “I request the Great King Vaiśravaṇa.
He then spoke this mantra:

*Namo vaiśravaṇāya | namo dhanadāya | dhanīśvarāya | ajita | aparājita | dhanīśvara | prama | kāruṇika | sarvasattvahitārthakara | mama [name] dāna | manupralayā kṣaya-majjita | svāhā.* “Once this mantra has been recited seven times in full...”
The instruction below requests protection.
First, the request is indicated; second, the mantra is recited; and finally, from "Recite this mantra seven times" onwards, the method of recitation is concluded.
Sūtra: "Next, recite the root mantra."

When wishing to recite the mantra, one should first invoke the names [of the deities], pay homage to the Triple Gem and the Great King Vaiśravaṇa—who can bestow wealth and cause the aspirations of all sentient beings to be fulfilled, and who is able to accomplish all things and grant them peace and happiness.
Having thus paid homage, one next recites the Heart Mantra of the King Vaiśravaṇa’s Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, which can bestow upon sentient beings peace and happiness according to their wishes.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa spoke before the Buddha the Heart Mantra of the Wish-Fulfilling Maṇi Jewel,
saying: "Namo ratnatrayāya."
Namo vaiśravaṇāya mahārājāya tadyathā si mi si mi.
Sūmu sūmu canda canda vajra vajra.
Sara sara kara kara kiri kiri.
Kuru kuru muru muru julu julu.
Svāhā! May I, named [so-and-so], attain [this]. Nidhanam astu.
Dada duṣṭāya svāhā | namo vaiśravaṇāya svāhā.
Dānadhye svāhā manoratha-paripūrakāya.

" Svāhā. Before receiving and maintaining the mantra, one should first recite it one thousand times. Thereafter, within a clean room, smear the ground with *gomaya* (cow dung) to create a small altar. At all times, provide offerings of food and drink with single-minded devotion, constantly burning exquisite incense so that the smoke does not cease. Recite the aforementioned heart-mantra day and night, binding the mind to it; let it be heard only by your own ears and do not allow others to understand it.
Next is the third section, the core mantra of the authentic teaching, which has four parts:
first, the introductory indication;
second, the instruction to first pay homage and make vows; [third, the actual mantra; fourth, the concluding benefits].
Third, command the recitation of the root mantra, beginning with "Having thus paid homage, next recite Vaiśravaṇa... and so forth;
fourth, from "At that time, the Heavenly King of Much Learning (Vaiśravaṇa)... onwards is the actual exposition of the mantra.
*Hratana* means "jewel" (*ratna*) in this [Chinese] language; *traya* means "three. This refers to paying homage to the Three Jewels.

What follows—*dāna* meaning "wealth," *deya* meaning "giving," *manas* meaning "mind/intention," *raha-pratā* meaning "I," and *pūraka* meaning "fulfilling"—collectively conveys the sense: "May the giving of wealth fulfill my intention."
The section beginning with "When receiving and upholding the mantra" explains the method for reciting the mantra.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, there was a prince of the Vaiśravaṇas named Caṇḍīśa, who appeared in the form of a youth and came to his [the practitioner's] side, asking:
'For what reason must you summon my father?'"
He should then reply:
"I require wealth and goods for the purpose of making offerings to the Triple Gem; I pray that you will grant them to me.
When the master artisan heard these words, he returned to his father's place and said to him:
"Now there is a virtuous person who has given rise to a heart of utmost sincerity to make offerings to the Triple Gem;
lacking sufficient wealth, he has issued this invitation.
His father replied, "You may go quickly and give him one hundred *kāṛṣāpaṇas* every day"—this is the original Sanskrit term (*kāṛṣāpaṇa*), which is seen here only as "mouth-teeth" (*mukha-danta*).
Furthermore, these vary by region and are not fixed; they may be cowrie shells, or coins made of gold, silver, copper, iron, and so forth.
However, in Magadha today, one *kāṛṣāpaṇa* is commonly used as equivalent to one thousand six hundred cowrie shells, and the total number can be calculated accordingly.
If one calculates it by its value, the amount varies depending on the location.
If a person achieves success through the recitation of this mantra, they will know the quantity themselves at the time they receive the goods.
One version of the text states: "Every day, one hundred *cennaras* shall be given," which refers to gold coins; thus, one shall obtain them daily until the end of one's life.
"In the Western regions, those who seek [this practice] often experience divine efficacy, provided they do not lack sincerity of heart.

Once the mantra-holder has seen these signs and knows that the task will be accomplished, he must stay alone in a clean room, burn incense, and sleep. He should place a casket of incense by his bedside; every at dawn, he shall look into the casket and obtain the object he seeks. Whenever an object is obtained, he must on that very day offer incense, flowers, and food to the Triple Gem, and simultaneously give it all away to the poor until nothing remains; it must not be kept back.

Give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings; do not harbor thoughts of anger, deception, flattery, or malice. If anger arises, the spiritual efficacy will be lost; therefore, one should always guard the mind and prevent it from becoming resentful.
The following clarifies the benefits obtained from the mantra, which are twofold:
first, the benefit seen in the son of Much-Learning; second, the benefit seen in King Much-Learning.
Within the benefit seen in the son, there are five parts:
1. A prince comes and asks;
2. From "Then he may reply" onwards, the mantra-holder answers;
3. From "At that time, the master Śāṇavāsin" onwards, the son returns and informs his father.
IV. From "His father replied" onwards, the father orders his son to give [the mantra]. V.

The commentary states:
Within the section on Dharmapāla’s defense, this is the third major section, the World-Honored One’s praise.
This praise consists of:
The first part praises the benefit for sentient beings; the section beginning with "Furthermore, this sutra" praises the benefit for the Dharma.

The Sutra says: At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rose from their seats, bared one shoulder, prostrated at his feet, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, praised the Buddha’s merits with sublime verses:

"The Buddha's face is like the pure, full moon, And like a thousand suns emitting radiance; His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses, His teeth are white, even, and closely set like jade or snow."

The Buddha’s virtues are boundless like the great ocean; within it, infinite wondrous jewels are amassed. The waters of wisdom and merit are ever full, and hundreds of thousands of supreme concentrations completely fill it.

The marks of the wheels upon your feet are all exquisitely adorned; the hub, the rim, and the thousand spokes are perfectly even. Your hands and feet are fully embellished with webbing, just as the king of geese is endowed with these marks.

The Buddha’s body radiates brilliance like a mountain of gold; pure, extraordinary, and without peer, it is also like Mount Sumeru, replete with merit. Therefore, I bow my head to the Buddha, King of Mountains.

Your marks and signs are like space, unfathomable; surpassing a thousand moons, you radiate brilliant light. All are like flames or illusions, inconceivable; therefore, I bow my head with a mind free from attachment.
Commentary: Within the third major section of this chapter, "The Four Kings Bearing Gratitude and Praising the Buddha," there are two parts:
The first part consists of the prose section praising the ritual protocol for the Buddha, followed by the formal verses.
While the preceding praise of the mantra mentioned only extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), the current praise applies universally to all four kings.
Because it is intended that focused supplication will easily bring success, the mantra is recited only once.
Because hearing the Dharma brings benefit through supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*), the Four Heavenly Kings all offer praise.
Furthermore, because the Buddha alone is able to preach the sūtras, they praise only the Buddha and not others.
There are five verses in total:
the first four verses separately praise the marks and signs, and the final verse praises them collectively and offers salutation.
Within the separate praise, there are two parts:
First is the praise, followed by one line of homage.
Within the praise there are seven parts:
half a verse praises the features of the face, one line the eyes, and one line the teeth.

The first verse describes the great ocean of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as a whole; the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth, are its wondrous jewels.

Wisdom is the foundation, like water; meditative concentration relies upon wisdom. This is because, in the state of Buddhahood, wisdom is predominant—just as a great cloud of Dharma-wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues.
One half-verse describes the mark of the wheel on the soles; one half-verse describes the mark of the webbed fingers.
Three lines describe the mark of the body’s radiance; one line expresses prostration.
Following the section on "marks and signs" (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) in the Sūtra, there is a general praise in two parts:
The first three phrases are praise, and the final phrase is prostration.
Within these three phrases, the first is general, while the latter two concern light. Furthermore, there is another interpretation:

The first verse praises the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); the next verse praises the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body); the following two verses offer praise for both the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* together; and the final verse praises the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

Within the description of the *dharmakāya*, one line indicates its essence, two lines indicate the arising of the functions of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, and the final line expresses veneration.
Sūtra: At that time, after the Four Heavenly Kings had praised the Buddha, the World-Honored One also replied to them in verse, saying:

"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* was spoken by the Unsurpassed One of Ten Powers; you, the Four Kings, shall always protect and guard it, and you should give rise to a courageous and non-regressive mind."
This wondrous jewel of a sutra is exceedingly profound; it is able to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings.
Because those sentient beings find such peace and joy, this sutra shall always circulate throughout Jambudvīpa.
Within this great trichiliocosm, all classes of sentient beings—whether hungry ghosts, animals, or those in the hells—all such realms of suffering are entirely eliminated.

The kings who dwell in this Southern Continent, as well as all other classes of sentient beings, shall always rejoice through the power of this sutra; may they all receive protection and attain peace and security, and likewise may the sentient beings herein be freed from manifold diseases and sufferings, and be rid of thieves and robbers.
"Because this land propagates the sutra, it shall be peaceful, secure, abundant, and joyful, free from conflict or affliction.

This consists of fifteen verses, which are further divided into four sections:

The multitudes of devas in this world, numbering beyond measure and inconceivable, all together listen to and receive this King of Sutras, joyfully upholding it without ever regressing.

If a person listens to and receives this King of Sutras, they will possess majestic virtue and valor, remaining forever sovereign; they shall increase the welfare of all beings among gods and humans, causing them to leave behind decline and affliction and to gain increased radiance.

The final verse serves as the concluding summary:

Because the deva has obtained increase, he is free from the signs of the five types of decline—both major and minor—and his radiance is constantly augmented.
Sūtra: At that time, having heard these verses, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as they addressed the Buddha, saying:

Since the distant past, we have never before heard such profound and subtle sounds. Our hearts were moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy; our tears flowed profusely and our entire bodies trembled as we realized this inconceivable and rare event.”
They scattered divine *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers over the Buddha.
Having made this sublime offering to the Buddha, they addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We four kings each have five hundred yakṣa attendants who shall constantly protect this sūtra and the Dharma-preacher in every place, providing assistance and defense through the light of wisdom.

Regarding any points of meaning in this sutra that they may have forgotten, I shall cause them all to remember them without forgetfulness, and I shall grant them the sublime Dharma-gate of dhāraṇī so that they may attain it in its entirety.

Furthermore, it is intended that this most supreme King of Sutras, wherever it may be, shall be widely proclaimed and disseminated for the sake of all sentient beings, so that it does not quickly disappear.

This is the fifth major section, "The Four Kings Rejoice and Protect."

Second, from the section "Addressing the Buddha" onwards, he speaks to present his petition; this has three sub-parts:
First, hearing what has never been heard before;

second, the body and mind are filled with joy—according to the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), a Bodhisattva of the first stage acts as a Four Heavenly King; having attained the realization of non-retrogression, upon hearing the profound Dharma, they weep with a mixture of sorrow and joy and their entire body trembles;
third, attaining what was never attained before, which is the realization of inconceivable matters.
3. From "With celestial *mandārava* flowers" below, there is the offering of scattered flowers.
4. From "Performing this sublime [act]" below, there is the request for protection and sustenance, which has two parts:
first, protection of the body;...
Regarding the section beginning with "By the light of wisdom," there are three ways in which wisdom provides protection:

Sūtra: At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma amidst the great assembly, immeasurable sentient beings all attained great wisdom, sagacity, and eloquence; they gathered an immeasurable mass of merit, were freed from all afflictions and distress, gave rise to a mind of joy and bliss, became well-versed in various treatises, ascended the path of transcendence, never again regressed, and swiftly realized Bodhi.
The sixth major section, "The Great Assembly Hearing the Sūtra and Attaining Benefits," has nine parts:

Chapter Thirteen: The Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment (Five Manuscripts). Chapter Thirteen: The Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment. This chapter is analyzed according to three sections:
first, the purpose; second, the explanation of the title; third, the resolution of difficulties.

Regarding the intent of this discourse: the sixteen chapters following the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings Observing Humans and Devas" first clarify the circulation of study and practice, which consists of five parts:

first, the "Observation Chapter," which exhorts the cultivation of practice; second, the three chapters beginning with the "Four Heavenly Kings Protecting the Nation Chapter," which clarify protection; third, the five chapters beginning with the "Great Eloquence Chapter," which clarify the increase of merit and wisdom for those who propagate the sutra; fourth, the three chapters beginning with the "Treatise on the Righteousness of Royal Law," which clarify the correct maintenance of study; and fifth, the four chapters beginning with the "Prediction of Attainment," which fulfill the aforementioned intents of exhorting practice and protection.
Within the three chapters beginning with "The Four Kings Protecting the Nation," which clarify protection, there are three parts:

first, causing them to protect and make offerings; second, causing them to remain free from defilement and not regress; and third, causing them to be free from obstacles and have their wishes fulfilled.
The preceding section clarified guarding and making offerings; this section clarifies causing one to remain free from defilement and not regress.
If there is attachment, there will be regression and despondency, because of such clinging.

As stated by Bodhisattva Asaṅga in his *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, regarding the explanation of abandoning the obstacle of intolerance for suffering: "Not abiding in any phenomena while generating the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and so forth, serves as the remedy for the suffering of cyclic existence, the suffering of adverse conditions, and the suffering of the lack of resources for enjoyment."

The present case is also like this; therefore, the subsequent passage states: "If bodhisattvas are able to abide [in this], they shall no longer regress from unsurpassed enlightenment, they will fulfill their correct vows, attain the eloquence of intrinsic nature which is without dependence, and achieve rare wonders while abiding in the noble path."
Therefore, this mantra was taught to protect [practitioners] so that they may remain free from defilement and not regress in their cultivation; it is because of this that this chapter arises.

Second, regarding the explanation of the title: in Sanskrit it is called *Vimalaprabhā*, which here means "Stainless Radiance" (*Wú rǎnzhù*); the old translation as "Lord of Silver" (*Yín zhǔ*) is incorrect.

The Dharma that is propagated flows equally from the most pure dharma-realm; furthermore, by the power of the mantra, it can cause one to be free from defilement and without attachment, and is therefore called "unstained and unattached."
Regarding *dhāraṇī*, its meaning is as commonly explained.
As for the "threefold resolution of difficulties," the question is:
Since there are four types of *dhāraṇī* in total, which *dhāraṇī* is this "absence of attachment"?

Answer: This is because it enables a bodhisattva to attain the *dhāraṇī* of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 45, states: "How does a bodhisattva attain the bodhisattva’s *dhāraṇī* of patience?"

This refers to those bodhisattvas who have accomplished a firm and stable practice of patience within their own being, who are endowed with sublime wisdom, and who—even without hearing it from others—have personally and correctly realized the meaning of all phenomena.

That is to say, one thus penetrates this meaning: that the referents of the intrinsic natures of all phenomena expressed by all verbal designations are not established as real, and there exists only the ineffable intrinsic nature of phenomena, and so forth.

Since this sutra states that what is called a *dhāraṇī* is not a location, and even goes so far as to say that there is no dharma that arises and no dharma that ceases, we know it is indeed this [teaching].
Or it refers to divine mantras and dhāraṇīs; as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "What is the bodhisattva’s mantra-dhāraṇī?

It means that bodhisattvas attain such mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that they empower various mantra phrases capable of removing the calamities and afflictions of sentient beings, causing those phrases to be entirely efficacious and able to eliminate many kinds of diverse misfortunes."
Furthermore, this sutra states: "The body shall also not be harmed by swords, staves, poisons, water, fire, or fierce beasts. Therefore, it is subsumed under divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*).
Alternatively, it may apply to both [categories], as the text contains no distinction between them.
Question:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "The essence of the four dhāraṇīs is not exclusively mindfulness and wisdom; the dhāraṇī of divine mantras is said to be meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the dhāraṇī of attaining patience (*kṣānti*) is said to be sublime wisdom (*prajñā*)."
"How is that so? Answer: "Because their essential natures are different."
When its essence arises based on reliance upon causes, it is called concentration (*samādhi*);
when its essence arises based on reliance upon the ability to discern, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*);
and when its essence arises based on reliance upon memory, it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
There is a resultant fruit that manifests as a substance, which is precisely what is called "dhāraṇī" (total retention) when referring to the dharmas it sustains.
Each [definition] relies on a specific meaning, yet none of them contradict one another.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains dhāraṇī as follows: "Because one attains the fire of wisdom through meditative concentration."

It is further said: "Wisdom, when it resides within the mind of a bodhisattva, is called *prajñā*; when it resides within the mind of one of the Lesser Vehicle, it is called the *mārgāṅga* (factors of the path); and when it resides within the mind of one who does not forget [the teachings], it is called *dhāraṇī*."

Thus we know that when the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states, "Dhāraṇīs of incantations (*mantra*) are said to be concentration (*samādhi*), while dhāraṇīs of patience (*kṣānti*) are called wisdom (*prajñā*)," each is spoken according to its specific meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the statement within the section on incantation-dhāraṇīs, "Because one attains such mastery over meditative absorption (*samādhi*), divine incantations become efficacious," this is spoken in reference to the cause and does not describe their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states: "Attainments are of three kinds:
first, those obtained through retribution;
second, those obtained through practice, because they are attained by the power of present hearing and retention."
"Third is 'attainment through cultivation,' because it is obtained by relying on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

From this, one should know that when it is said that such spells empowered by mastery over meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are all efficacious, it is because one has attained concentration and thus gives rise to superior mindfulness and wisdom capable of upholding the various spells; this defines their essential nature (*svabhāva*) in terms of their cause."

Regarding "attaining the dhāraṇī of patience": patience is the fruit and the mantra is the cause of patience. Because one maintains this mantra for attaining patience through the power of mindfulness and wisdom, it is called the Bodhisattva’s Dhāraṇī for Attaining Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Both the mantra that is maintained and the essence that maintains it have mindfulness and wisdom as their substance.

Alternatively, it may be that only the capacity to maintain [the mantra] constitutes its essence, with mindfulness and wisdom as its substance, while the maintained mantra itself is not; this is like using dharani to maintain words and meanings, for the maintained words and meanings are not themselves mindfulness and wisdom.
Alternatively, the mantra is the cause; by the power of this mantra, one is able to attain the four kinds of *dhāraṇī*, thereby upholding those four dharmas so as not to forget them.

Furthermore, when the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "attaining the *dhāraṇī* of patience is sublime wisdom," this is also spoken in terms of the cause. It says: "Bodhisattvas achieve a firm and solid patience within their own being and are endowed with sublime wisdom, dwelling alone in seclusion, silent and without speech. It continues: "Regarding the mantric phrases of the Bodhisattva-patience attained from the Buddha's teachings, they are able to contemplate them with precision; such meanings of these phrases are realized through independent penetration without hearing them from others, understanding that these mantric phrases are entirely devoid of [conventional] meaning," and so forth.
To speak of "accomplishing the practice of firm patience": the practitioner is the cause, and this cause is sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because one has attained sublime wisdom, dwelling alone in seclusion, silent and without speech, constitutes both the locus of practice and the mode of practice.

Regarding the mantra phrases and so forth taught by the Buddha for attaining the bodhisattva’s patience (*kṣānti*), these are the dharmas to be studied that serve as the causes for attaining patience.
One who is able to contemplate them is one who is able to practice; this is precisely the cause.

Therefore, the *Vyūha-śāstra* states: "Because it is attained through the power of manifest hearing and retention. Thus, we know that the name *dhāraṇī* does not refer solely to the total retention of mindfulness and wisdom; rather, the causes of such total retention—namely mindfulness and wisdom—as well as the dharmas they retain, are all also called *dhāraṇī*. Consequently, both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and mantras are termed *dhāraṇī*.

Furthermore, the dharma-meaning (*dharmārtha*) that is upheld is the general [factor], while the divine mantra (*vidyā-mantra*) and the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*) are the specific [factors], because both the divine mantra and the mantra obtained through patience likewise possess the quality of dharma-meaning.
Question:

If it is said that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are the causes for dhāraṇī, why does the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* state: "If bodhisattvas possess four qualities, they will then obtain dhāraṇī; it is not the case that they may lack even one"?
Answer: Because there are proximate and remote causes, concentration and wisdom are the proximate causes.

As for those four causes: first, non-attachment to sensual desires; second, being free from envy toward others' excellence; third, feeling no regret regarding equal giving; and fourth, generating deep joy and aspiration for the True Dharma—these four are the remote causes.
Question:
At what stage are these four dhāraṇīs attained? Answer:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Because they have attained this patience (*kṣānti*), these bodhisattvas will before long attain the bodhisattva-dharma-dhāraṇī and the meaning-dhāraṇī (*artha-dhāraṇī*) of the stage of pure superior intention (*viśuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*)."
Once one has passed beyond the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and entered the stage of the pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), what is attained is definitive.
Although [qualities] may be attained prior to this, they are not definitive, as explained in the *Dharmārtha-sūtra*.
"You should know that it is the same for the dhāraṇī-mantras.
Based on this, it follows that the *dhāraṇī* of attaining patience (*kṣānti-labdha*) is acquired prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), while the others are acquired upon entering the stages.

However, speaking according to reality, if one considers their relative superiority or inferiority and their completeness or deficiency, the levels at which they are attained are not necessarily fixed in that way.

As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts, one attains the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining (*śrutadhāraṇī*) in the third bhūmi; it is also said that one attains the four dhāraṇīs in the ninth bhūmi.
If categorized by initial realization of the principle, both are attained in the first bhūmi;
if categorized by attainment through cultivation, both are common to the stages prior to the bhūmis;
if categorized by spontaneous attainment, both occur from the eighth bhūmi upward.

Now, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that [the stage of] patience is attained prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), while others are attained upon entering them; these are mutually indicative of one another.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

"There is now a Dharma-gate named the *Anupalipta-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment). This is the Dharma practiced by all Bodhisattvas, that which was upheld by Bodhisattvas of the past, and it is the mother of Bodhisattvas."
Having spoken these words, he commented: "The main text is divided into six sections:

first, the Buddha designates the title and the essential doctrine; second, the inquiry and response regarding the name and substance; third, the request for the Buddha to expound it; fourth, the praise and aspiration for its proclamation; fifth, the manifestation of its excellence and exhortation to practice; and sixth, the joy in hearing the teaching and the resolve to study."
This is the first [section].
There are seven parts:
the first clarifies the Teacher.
Second, the capacity of those to be guided;
third, the designation of the mantra's name;
fourth, the indication of what should be studied.
Five, the citation of previous exhortations;
six, clarifying the intent of study—because this is the mother of bodhisattvas, because all past bodhisattvas have already studied it, and because it is what present bodhisattvas ought to practice;
seven, the conclusion of the preceding heading.
The passage may be fully understood from the sutra.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of the term *dhāraṇī*,
World-Honored One?
World-Honored One, a *dhāraṇī* is neither a location nor a non-location."
Having spoken these words,
he proceeds to inquire about the names and essences through a series of questions and answers, with the question first and the answer last.
Within the question, there are two parts:
First, regarding the meaning of the name:
what is the semantic content of this phrase, and in what sense is it called "Non-attachment" (Aśvaghoṣa) and so forth?
Furthermore, for what reason is the *pada* (phrase) the expressive name, rather than the name being contained within the *nāma-pada* (name-phrase)?

The following questions concern the essence [of the dhāraṇī]: since the essence of all phenomena is suchness (tathatā), which is neither existent nor empty and is ineffable, how can this dhāraṇī be explained?
"Not being a spatial location" means being free from existence; "not being a non-spatial location" means being free from emptiness.
According to the Buddha’s response below, there are seven phrases; here, the first phrase is briefly cited as a question to serve as an illustration for the remainder.
Alternatively, it is because Śāriputra has attained partial awakening while the World-Honored One has attained complete awakening that there is said to be a difference in degree.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
"Śāriputra! You have already set out upon the Mahāyāna; you believe in and understand the Mahāyāna, and you hold the Mahāyāna in high esteem.
This response below consists of two parts:
First the praise, then the response.
This is the praise.
It consists of two parts:
The words "Excellent! constitute a praise for the inquiry.
The section beginning with "Regarding you in the Mahāyāna" praises his virtues, which are threefold:
first, it praises his abandonment of the Lesser Vehicle, as he has already been able to set out upon the Great Path.
Next is the praise for awakening to the Great [Vehicle], because of having faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) in the Mahāyāna.

Since this is an entry through the attainment of understanding by means of faith, rather than an entry through the realization of wisdom, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Śāriputra, you have already entered this sutra through faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas."
After entering the Great Vehicle, one passes through twenty thousand kalpas before first reaching the initial stage of the Ten Faiths.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Arhats reach it after twenty thousand kalpas."
Regarding what was said about "reaching," it refers to reaching the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, one has not yet attained realization.

If categorized according to the seven stages (*bhūmi*), having transcended the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), one resides in the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

If categorized according to the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*), one who has not yet entered the stage of provisioning (*sambhārāvasthā*) but merely possesses a desire for wholesome dharmas is only then able to enter the stage of provisioning upon attaining the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The subsequent praise of "firmness" is because of their profound respect for the Mahāyāna.

Sūtra: "As you have said, that which is called *dhāraṇī* is neither a location nor a non-location; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither a thing nor a non-thing; it is neither a condition nor a non-condition; it is neither activity nor non-activity; there is no dharma that arises therein, nor is there any dharma that ceases."
The response below has two parts:
first, the answer regarding the essence; second, from "that is all Buddhas" onwards, the answer regarding the meaning of the name.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
The first part presents the established argument; the latter part, beginning with "However, for the sake of... and so forth, answers by explaining the reason.
The first part presents the established argument.
That it is not a spatial location and so forth has already been explained previously.
The second, "unrighteousness and so forth," is free from both the signifier and the signified.

It is not unrighteousness, for it is not that which is signified; nor is it not unrighteousness, for it is not something that is not free from being non-signified, because it is realized through gnosis.
Third, it is apart from the three periods of time; because it is eternal, it does not belong to the three periods.
It must therefore be that which is neither past nor the others, for it is not a phenomenon that is apart from time; this is stated by way of abbreviation.
The seventh sentence of the sutra is also explained in this same way.
Regarding the fourth point, the correspondence between principle and phenomenon:
it is principle and not phenomenon; yet it is said to be "not non-phenomenon" because it does not depart from phenomenal dharmas.
The fifth is the counterpart of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

It is not conditioned because it does not arise through dependent origination, yet it is not non-conditioned because it is manifested by a revealing cause, or because it is not separate from dharmas that arise through dependent origination.
The sixth is the pair of permanence and impermanence:
the practitioner undergoes flux, whereas True Suchness (tathatā) is neither conditioned activity nor non-activity; this is explained as before.
The seventh is the pair of characteristics and non-characteristics.
Because the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from the ten marks such as arising and ceasing, the essence of all phenomena arises; what follows after this is called cessation.
Since there is no arising according to suchness, there is likewise no cessation of phenomena; this example is cited to illustrate the rest.
The seventh [point] is the departure from the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
This refers to the understanding of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) among the three natures, as it is that to which all phenomena ultimately tend.
If considered in terms of the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the seven phrases of the ultimate truth provide a comprehensive negation.
If we consider the two truths in relation to one another, they generally encompass both negation and affirmation.

For example, regarding "not being a spatial location": from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it negates being a spatial location while affirming that it is neither a spatial location nor a non-spatial location. From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because the phenomena sustained by the essence of the dhāraṇī are dependent upon sound, the intrinsic nature of the dhāraṇī consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
Mindfulness and wisdom are not spatial, because they depend upon spatial locations; the rest may be understood by analogy.

However, according to the intent of the sūtras, with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the path of verbal expression is cut off. Taking this in its entirety—both through negation and affirmation—it does not rely on the dependent nature (*paratantra*) or the imagined nature (*parikalpita*). Alternatively, it may apply to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) without any fault.
Sūtra: "However, for the sake of benefiting all bodhisattvas, it is thus spoken; herein, the efficacy, the correct principle, the approach, and the power [of this dhāraṇī] are established."
The following answer explains the reason for this.

However, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is neither a spatial location nor a non-spatial location; it transcends words and is devoid of characteristics. Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting all bodhisattvas, such a statement is made here within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by relying on the principles of skillful means (*upāya*).
On what basis is the Dharma taught?
It refers to the very essence of the Dharma being taught within this dhāraṇī.
It is called "teaching" because it is established and designated based upon four kinds of meanings.
Regarding the term "establishment" (*vyavasthāna*) mentioned below, it refers to the designation of specific names based on these four meanings.
As for the four types of meaning: first is "function" (*kāritra*), which is explained as the function capable of attaining the fruit based upon the total retention (*dhāraṇī*).

Second is the right path (*samyag-mārga*); that is, the essence of this functional activity is called the "right path" because it realizes the correct principle by remaining free from the two extremes, consisting of mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth.

Third is the principle (*naya*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*) and the meanings of the dharmas supported by it; these are the objects of mindfulness and knowledge, collectively termed "principle."

The four powers: because through these dharmas and their meanings one can exercise mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth, extinguishing evil, generating good, realizing principle, and attaining the fruit, they are called "powers"; that is, the majestic power of the Dharma.
This is intended to clarify that the expressive designations accord with all phenomena.

Alternatively, it refers to the two factors of dhāraṇī and mindfulness-wisdom, which possess the power to sustain and uphold [the teachings], giving rise to the wholesome and extinguishing the unwholesome.

Sūtra: “This is the merit of all Buddhas, the prohibitions and precepts of all Buddhas, that which all Buddhas study, the secret intent of all Buddhas, and the place of birth of all Buddhas; therefore, it is named the Most Sublime Dharma Gate of the Unstained Adherence Dhāraṇī.”
Having spoken these words, he provides the answer to the question.
The first part, "therefore it is called 'untainted,'" answers the meaning; the subsequent part answers the phrasing.

The "phrase" (*pada*) is synonymous with the "name" (*nāman*). The four preceding meanings—such as "function" (*prayoga*) and so forth—reside in the Buddha; thus, they are collectively termed "merit" (*guṇa*) and so on.

Alternatively, because it can serve as a cause, based upon which one attains the Buddha's unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), it is termed "merit"; because it enables the abandonment of faults, it is termed "prohibitory precept" (*śīla*); because it serves as the Teacher of the Buddha, it is termed "that which is to be studied" (*śikṣā*); because the wondrous principle of the Dharma-body is profound and difficult to fathom, it is termed "secret intent" (*rahasya*); and because it brings about the Reward and Transformation Buddhas, it is termed "place of birth" (*janmasthāna*).
Because these meanings are expressed by the teaching that articulates them, they are called "the dharma-gate of non-attachment" and so forth.
Alternatively, mindfulness and wisdom themselves are called "dharma-gates," as they serve as the gates for the dharmas they uphold; thus, they are the gates to the Dharma.
Alternatively, based on this dhāraṇī, one can produce merits and so forth;

thus, it is the "gate of the sublime Dharma. Alternatively, this sublime Dharma encompasses both the producer and the produced; thus, it admits of both the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analyses.
Sūtra. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Sugata will explain this dharma of dhāraṇī for me.”

If bodhisattvas are able to abide therein, they will no longer regress from unsurpassed enlightenment and will accomplish their right vows; they will attain independent, intrinsic eloquence, achieve rare and marvelous qualities, and dwell securely in the noble path—all because they have obtained this dhāraṇī.
The third section, "Requesting the Buddha to Expound," has two parts:
first, the actual request for the teaching; second, the underlying intent of the request, which itself has two aspects.
First, those who are able to learn; second, from "those who are able to abide securely" onwards, it clarifies the benefits obtained through practicing the teachings.
There are six [points]:
first, attaining non-retrogression, which refers to the four types of non-retrogression, such as abiding according to faith and so forth.
Second is attaining the correct vows, namely the ten great vows.

The *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* states: "First, may the roots of goodness planted by me in previous lives and in this present life be bestowed upon all beings and collectively dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi; may this vow of mine increase in every thought-moment and remain unforgotten in every birth, being protected by dhāraṇīs."

Second, may I, having dedicated [this merit] toward great enlightenment, through these roots of goodness always obtain offerings to all Buddhas in every place of birth, and never be born in a land where no Buddha dwells.

Third, I pray that once I have been born in the lands of all Buddhas, I may always remain in close proximity and attend upon them at their side, like a shadow following a form, never being separated from the Buddhas for even a single moment.

Fourth, he made the vow: "Once I have drawn near to the Buddha, may He preach the Dharma to me according to what is appropriate for me, so that I may immediately achieve the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.

Fifth, he vowed: "Having attained these powers, may I immediately penetrate the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of provisional designations as they circulate in the world, and realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to attain the wisdom of the True Dharma."

Sixth, I vow that once I have attained the wisdom of the True Dharma, I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of all living beings with an insatiable mind, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them so that they may all achieve understanding.

Seventh, I vow that once I have brought all sentient beings to understanding, I shall, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas, listening to and receiving the True Dharma, and extensively gathering in all sentient beings.

Eighth, having heard the True Dharma authorized by all Buddhas, I shall immediately be able to turn the pure Wheel of Dharma; may all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my Dharma or hear my name immediately abandon all afflictions and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Ninth, may I be able to cause all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta; having done so, may I always follow and protect them, removing what is unbeneficial, bestowing immeasurable happiness, and sacrificing my body, life, and wealth to gather in sentient beings and shoulder the burden of the True Dharma.

Tenth: May I be able to shoulder the true Dharma; though practicing the true Dharma, may my mind have nothing to practice. Just as all bodhisattvas practice the true Dharma without practicing anything and yet without not practicing, I shall not abandon my right vows in order to transform sentient beings.
This is largely identical in meaning to the "Vow" section of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Third, attaining that which is without dependence refers to non-abiding nirvana.
Fourth, natural eloquence refers to the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
Because it is realized without depending on a teacher, it is called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, because these four types of eloquence arise for the benefit of others without having a [prior] cause, they are called "intrinsic nature.

Fifth, regarding the attainment of rare and marvelous things, according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, chapter forty-six, it says: "When a bodhisattva cultivates unsurpassed enlightenment, there are five marvelous and rare qualities:"
First, they give rise to affection for sentient beings without any causal conditions;
second, solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they constantly remain within saṃsāra and endure immeasurable suffering;
third, regarding sentient beings who have many afflictions and are difficult to subdue, they are skillfully able to understand the means of their discipline.
Fourth, they are able to progressively awaken to and enter the true meaning of the principles that are extremely difficult to understand;
fifth, they possess inconceivable great majestic spiritual power.

Sixth, they abide securely in the noble path: by abiding in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and attaining the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, they are said to abide securely in the noble path.
Alternatively, there may be five [types]:
the attainment of eloquence based on no support and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) are combined into one.
It is called "based on no support" because it does not depend on external conditions; it is called "intrinsic nature" because its capacity is inherently able to benefit others.
First, one may initially attain the stage of non-retrogression;
second, one attains the correct vows at the first bhūmi;
third, one attains the path of non-differentiation at the fifth bhūmi, which is called "attaining that which is without dependence."
Fourth, in the ninth stage, one attains the fourfold eloquence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pratibhāna*).
Fifth, in the tenth stage, one obtains rare and marvelous events.

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, regarding the marvelous events in the tenth stage, when the samādhi manifests, there appears a great king of jewel-lotuses, ten *asaṃkhyeya* yojanas in circumference, adorned with an interlacing array of all kinds of jewels; at that time, the body of the bodhisattva is exceptionally sublime, being commensurate with the lotus seat.
Sixth, one abides in the noble path at the stage of Buddhahood;
because this abiding is free from further seeking or striving, it is called "abiding.
The phrase "all by virtue of attaining this" and so forth serves as the conclusion.
Sūtra: The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.”
The fourth section below, the Proclamation of the Seal of Praise, has three parts:
first, the praise of the seal; second, further eulogy; and third, the actual proclamation.
This first part may be understood [as follows].
Sūtra: "If there is a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī, it should be known that this person is no different from a Buddha;
if there is anyone who makes offerings to, respects, serves, and provides for this bodhisattva, it should be known that they are making offerings to the Buddha."
The subsequent praise consists of three parts:
first, the praise for those capable of realization;
second, from "If there are those who make offerings" onwards, the praise for those capable of making offerings.

One should refer to the subsequent passage, "By these causes and conditions, one obtains the unsurpassed fruit," which explains that there is no difference from the Buddha and that this constitutes making offerings to the Buddha.

Sūtra: “Śāriputra! If there are others who hear this dhāraṇī, receive, uphold, read, recite, and give rise to faith and understanding, they too should be respectfully honored and provided with offerings no differently than the Buddha.”
"By these causes and conditions, one attains the unsurpassed fruit.
The following section praises those who are able to study and those who make offerings;
the explanation of the text may be understood by analogy.
Sūtra. At that time, the World-Honored One then expounded for them this dhāraṇī, saying:

“Tadyathā | santarale | uttarale | susamparistite | sunama | suparistitanirśyabala | satyaparatiñña | suaroha | ñjanamati | upatani | avanamani | abhisatani | aviviyahara | śubhavati | suniśrita | bho guñja | abhyavadhā | svāhā. Thus he spoke.
Sūtra. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“Regarding this *Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment*, if there is a bodhisattva who can skillfully abide in it and correctly uphold it, you should know that for such a person, whether for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand kalpas, their rightly made vows shall never be exhausted, and their body shall not be harmed by swords, staves, poisons, water, fire, or fierce beasts.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
this *Dhāraṇī* of Non-Attachment is the mother of all Buddhas of the past, the mother of all Buddhas of the future, and the mother of all Buddhas of the present.
The fifth section below, "Manifesting Excellence and Encouraging Practice," has two parts:
first, praising the efficacy of the Dharma; second, comparing its superiority and inferiority.
Within the first part, there are seven sections:
First, the audience to whom it is addressed;
second, from "This mantra is stained by attachment" onwards, the indicated dharma that is praised;
third, from "If a bodhisattva" onwards, the person who is capable of learning it.

4. From "Able to dwell well" onwards, it clarifies the reliance upon cultivation and study; by being able to dwell well, one takes this mantra as the basis, thereby being able to correctly receive and uphold it, and rely upon it to give rise to the practice of the Dharma.
Rightly receiving the wisdom of hearing, and rightly upholding the wisdom of reflection and cultivation.
Fifth, regarding the section "One should know that this person" and below, there are two parts concerning the benefits obtained:
first, by internal integration, one is able to give rise to vows that are inexhaustible, because one attains non-retrogression.
The two bodies are likewise not subject to it.
Furthermore, they prevent external non-virtuous influences from invading.
Sixth, "For what reason? is an inquiry into the underlying cause.
7. [The passage] beginning with “Śāriputra” below explains the reason. Sūtra: “Śāriputra!

Suppose there were a person who, for countless eons, offered as a gift to the Buddhas the seven treasures filling ten *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms, and further provided them with various offerings of exquisite clothing, food, and drink; yet if another person were able to receive and uphold even a single phrase of this dhāraṇī, the merit produced by the latter would be many times greater than that of the former.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because this profound Dharma gate of the *Anupalipta-dhāraṇī* is the mother of all Buddhas.
Next, the comparative evaluation of superiority and inferiority is divided into four parts:
first, citing the merit of giving; second, the formal comparison; third, questioning the basis for superiority; and fourth, answering the reason why.
The phrasing may be understood by analogy.
When the Venerable Śāriputra and the great assembly had heard this Dharma, they were all filled with great joy and vowed to receive and uphold it.
The sixth major section: Rejoicing in the Teaching and Studying It. Chapter Fourteen:
The Jewel that Grants All Wishes (Five Manuscripts). Chapter Fourteen: The Jewel that Grants All Wishes. This chapter is analyzed according to three gates:
First, regarding the underlying intent, there are three types within the section on circulation:
First is the propagation through practice and conduct, which has five parts; among these, the second is protection for the sake of propagation.
This, in turn, has three sections:

first, causing [the Dharma] to be protected and offered; second, protecting it so that it remains free from defilement and does not decline; and third, protecting this mantra so that one is freed from calamities and all that is sought is fulfilled as desired.
As the preceding text has clearly elucidated [the necessity], this chapter is now produced.
Second, regarding the explanation of the name: in Sanskrit it is called *cintā*, which here is translated as "as one wishes" (*yìrúì*).
The original sound simply names it "thought" (*yì*); its meaning refers to the mental faculty of deliberation and calculation.
"Like" (tathā) means "added meaning.
"Maṇi" is translated here as "jewel"; this is the metaphor.
"Dhāraṇī" refers to the Dharma.
Just as a jewel can cause one to be free from all calamities and ensure that whatever is sought accords with one's heart’s desire, this mantra is likewise; it is thus named after its metaphor.

It should properly be called the "Chapter on the Cintāmaṇi-ratna Dhāraṇī," which is why it is later referred to as the "Divine Mantra of the Cintāmaṇi-ratna," the full wording having been abbreviated.
Another explanation is as follows:
this very dhāraṇī is called the "wish-fulfilling jewel" (cintāmaṇi); since the dharma is named after its metaphor, it is said that there is a dhāraṇī named the "wish-fulfilling jewel."
This name is not explained by the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*). Regarding the difficulty concerning the three explanations:

Question—The mantra spoken by the Lord Vajradhara is called "Unconquerable" (*Ajita*), and other explanations are also distinct; why then is it referred to solely as the "Chapter on the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel"?
Answer: There are two interpretations. One says:
The title of this chapter cannot be fully analyzed from its beginning alone.
A second interpretation states:

"The first two [verses] receive the general name, while the others follow their specific designations; however, according to the actual fact, they all deserve to be called 'Wish-Fulfilling Jewels' (cintāmaṇi) in their totality."
Question:
Among the four dhāraṇīs, which one is this general dhāraṇī? Answer:
This is the *dhāraṇī* of the mantra.
Question:
In the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," that which was spoken by the four kings is also called a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). What is the distinction between this and that?
Answer: Though the names are the same, their meanings differ, as can be understood from the text.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda amidst the great assembly, saying:
"You should know that there is a dhāraṇī named 'Wish-Fulfilling Jewel,' which distances one from all calamities and misfortunes, and is also capable of warding off all evil thunderbolts."
The commentary states:
The text of this chapter is divided into four sections: first, the Buddha’s teaching; second, the assembly’s discourse; third, the Buddha’s seal of approval; and fourth, the practice and observance.
Within the Buddha’s teaching, there are three parts:
First, the announcement of the consent to speak; second, the assembly’s desire to hear; third, the Buddha’s formal speaking for them.
Within the first [section], there are four parts:
first, indicating the name of the mantra; second, demonstrating its efficacy; third, addressing those who will recite it together; fourth, granting permission to set it forth.
These are the first two.
The sūtra states: "It was proclaimed together by the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
The following is the third announcement, stating that they spoke in agreement.

Sūtra: "At this time, within this sūtra, I shall likewise proclaim it for you, the great assembly; it can bring great benefit to humans and devas, and out of compassion for the world, it shall protect all beings and cause them to attain peace and happiness."
The fourth section below, "Granting Permission for the Recitation," has two parts:
first, granting permission for the recitation; second, from "Able to... onwards, clarifying the benefits.
Sutra: At that time, the great assembly and Ānanda, having heard the Buddha’s words, each with utmost sincerity gazed up at the World-Honored One and listened to receive the divine mantra.
The great assembly below delighted in hearing the sutra. The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively, all of you."

In this eastern direction, there is a king of lightening named Agada; in the southern direction, there is a king of lightning named Śatru; in the western direction, there is a king of lightning named Prabhūtaprabha; and in the northern direction, there is a king of lightning named Sutamani.
The Buddha’s actual discourse consists of four parts:
first, the naming of the King of Lightning; second, the benefits gained from hearing it; third, the actual recitation of the mantra; and fourth, the method for chanting the mantra.
This explains the name "lightning.
The sound produced by the clashing of clouds is called "thunder.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "It is like the sound of clouds."
The light that emerges is named "Lightning" (Dien), for it is the presiding deity of lightning named King (Wang).

According to the *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* (*Qishi jing*), it says: "In the east, the 'Immovable Lightning' (Wubian dien) and in the west, the 'Falling Radiant Lightning' (Duoguangming dien) strike, adhere, rub, and clash against one another. Because of this, within the clouds at the edge of the void, radiance is produced, which is called 'Immovable Lightning' (Bidian)."

"In the east is the one named Closed Lightning, called Wúhòu; in the south is the one called Following the Current; in the west is the one called Fallen Radiance; and in the north is the one called Hundred-Thousand Tree Lightning.
These names are established according to their presiding deities."
Regarding the differences in the names of this scripture, it may be that there are many deities, or that the translations differ.
*Ajita* means "come" (*āgata*) in this language;
*suta* means "like a mani-jewel," as explained previously.

Sūtra: "If there are good sons or good daughters who hear the names of such lightning kings and know their locations, these persons shall immediately be far removed from all matters of fear, and all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished."

If one writes down the names of these four directional kings of lightning within one’s dwelling, there will be no fear of thunder and lightning in that place; furthermore, calamities, misfortunes, and all obstructive afflictions will be absent, and untimely or unjust deaths will be entirely avoided.
The following clarifies the benefits gained, which are twofold:
first, the benefit of hearing the name; second, from "If, in one's dwelling place... onwards, it clarifies the benefit of writing down the name.
