Question: Since one is already freed from fear upon hearing the name of the King of Lightning, why is it necessary to recite a mantra in order to be freed from fear? Answer:
By the power of upholding the mantra, one can cause that king to provide protection and thereby free one from fear.
Furthermore, while the initial deity protects against fear and the subsequent mantra protects against fear, it is the mantra protection that is superior;
thus the chapter of the sutra is named after it.
Sutra: At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this mantra, saying:

*Tadyathā | nime nime | nime nime | nimindare | sthiralokālakanī | sthiraśūlabhāṇī | hūṃ kṣa hūṃ kṣa | May I, [Name], and all those dwelling in this place be entirely freed from every fear, all suffering and affliction, lightning, thunderbolts, and even untimely death. Svāhā.* [The following describes the mantra and the method for reciting it.]

Sūtra: At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, being amidst the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I shall now, before the Buddha, briefly proclaim this divine mantra of the wish-fulfilling jewel, which brings great benefit to all humans and devas; out of compassion for the world, it protects all beings and grants them peace and happiness, possessing great majestic power so that all requests are fulfilled as wished.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
"Tadyathā | hate | vihate | nihate..."
Pratitye pratidindi pratisire śuddhimukte vimale.
Praprasāhare antare bandhale kṣite bandharāvasini.
Hakṣe keta re kapi le piṅgala o kiṭa ti mukhi.

"Hakṣa hakṣa! May all terrors, sufferings, and even unjust deaths pertaining to me, [Name], and this entire dwelling be completely removed. May I never behold evil things, and may I always be protected and remembered by the majestic light of the Great Compassion of the Holy Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Svāhā! There are six mantras spoken by the assembly below:
The initial exposition by Avalokiteśvara consists of three parts:
first, the request for the teaching; second, the actual teaching; and third, the method for reciting the mantra.
The initial invitation consists of three parts:
first, the ritual of invitation; second, the request for the teaching;
and third, the description of its benefits. In Sanskrit, it is called *avalokiteśvarāya*.
*Āvalokiteśvara*: *Āvalokita* means "observing" (in Chinese), while others translate it as "sovereign.

Because he constantly observes the world with his divine eyes, divine ears, and the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, and is able to rescue beings accordingly, he is called Avalokiteśvara, or "Observing Sovereign."
Regarding the name "Avalokiteśvara," it is derived from a single [Sanskrit] term; as its name is not fully expressed here, it is not a literal translation.
This may be understood by cross-referencing the text.
[Sūtra]: At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now also proclaim a dhāraṇī mantra called ‘Unconquerable,’ which brings great benefit to all humans and devas, compassionately protects all in the world, possesses great majestic power, and fulfills all that is sought according to one's wishes.”
He then spoke the mantra:
“Tadyathā | muñce muñce | muṇili maditi maditi | sumati mahāmati | haha hahamaha paryanasiddhe pravarta | vajrapāṇi | akhaṇḍa jvalitaca svāhā. “World-Honored One! [he said.]

This divine mantra of mine is named "Invincible Protection. If there are men or women who single-mindedly receive, uphold, transcribe, recite, and remember it without forgetting, I shall constantly protect such persons day and night, ensuring they are entirely freed from all terrors, even including unjust death.
The second section below also consists of three parts:
first, the request for the teaching; second, the actual teaching; and third, the benefits of recitation and retention.
The allocation of these textual sections can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the term "Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets," some say that Avalokiteśvara assumes a different form and is thus called "Secret"; he constantly holds a vajra to protect the Triple Gem, and his name is derived from both himself and what he holds.
According to the *Guhyakapada-vajrapāṇi-sūtra*, this Vajradhara and the Brahmā King are each one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
It is as explained at length therein.
The sutra states: At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

I also possess a subtle dharma-gate of dhāraṇī, which brings great benefit to all humans and devas; out of compassion for the world, it protects all beings, possesses great majestic power, and fulfills whatever is sought according to one's wishes.
He then spoke the mantra:
“Tadyathā | hiri miri dhiri svāhā | varakamabūri | varakama-maṇi-varakama-garbhe | puṣpa-saṃsiddhare svāhā. “World-Honored One!

This divine mantra of mine is named "Brahma-Healing" (Brahmaviśuddhi); it is fully capable of protecting those who uphold this mantra, causing them to be free from sorrow and affliction, as well as all sinful karma, and ensuring that even premature death is entirely avoided.
The third exposition follows, with its textual structure identical to the preceding.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I also possess a dhāraṇī named Vajraśānti, a great vidyā-mantra capable of eliminating all terrors and calamities, even ensuring that one is entirely free from untimely death; it uproots suffering and bestows happiness, bringing benefit to humans and devas alike.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

"Tadyathā | vinipare | bandhamadane | manini ciciṇi gauri | gandhāri cāṇḍāli | mātaṅgi daśakasi | sarabhadre hīnamastuta modataraṇi | moharaṇi dāraṇi khaṅgacārapāki | śavari śavari | Svāhā. The fourth recitation below is also identical in text to the preceding.
Regarding the term "Lord Śakra": "Śakra" (帝) means "lord" (主), and "Śakra" (釋) means "able" (能); thus, it is translated here as "Able Lord" (能帝), which is the general designation.
As for the subsequent phrase "Lord of Devas" (天主), it means one who is able to act as the lord of devas.

Sūtra: At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa all rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now also possess a divine mantra named "Bestowing Fearlessness upon All Sentient Beings," which constantly provides protection against all suffering and affliction, enabling them to attain peace and happiness, increase their lifespan, and be free from all ailments and pain, even to the point of entirely avoiding untimely death.
He then spoke the mantra:

“Tadyathā | puṣpe | supuṣpe | dumaprahāre | āryapraśaste | śāntinirmukte maṅgale siddhe | siddhibuddhe | svāhā. This concludes the fifth section; it consists of two parts and lacks the benefits of recitation.
In the first section, there are three parts: first, the listing of names; second, the ritual of request; and third, the description of the benefits.
These can be understood by referring to the text.

The Sūtra says: At that time, there were also various great nāga kings—namely, the Nāga King Manasvin, the Nāga King Vidyutprabha, the Nāga King Anavatapta, the Nāga King Vidyujjihva, and the Nāga King Suprabha—who all rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I also possess a *dhāraṇī* of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), which can ward off evil lightning and eliminate all terrors; it brings great benefit to humans and devas, compassionately protects all in the world, and possesses great majestic power such that all requests are fulfilled as wished. It causes even untimely deaths to be entirely avoided, neutralizes all poisons, and eradicates all malevolent practices of sorcery, incantations, and inauspicious deeds.”
The sixth section below has three parts as previously stated.
The first part consists of five sections:
first, the listing of names; second, the ritual of the two requests beginning with "both rising from their seats"; and third, the description of the benefits.
Sūtra: “I now offer this divine mantra to the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will compassionately and mercifully accept it.
This concludes the fourfold request for acceptance.
Sūtra: “May we be led to leave this dragon realm and forever abandon stinginess and greed.”
Why is this? Because due to this stinginess and greed, one undergoes various sufferings and afflictions within the cycle of birth and death.
We vow to sever the seeds of stinginess and greed.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
“Tadyathā | Acche | Amale | Amṛte | Akṣaye | Abhaye | Punyapariyāyate | Sarvabhadrapratiśamane | Svāhā | Arice Pandusuparṇe | Svāhā. “World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who recite this dhāraṇī mantra with their mouths, or who copy it into a scroll, receive, uphold, read, recite, and reverently make offerings to it, they shall forever be free from lightning, thunderbolts, and all forms of fear, distress, sorrow, and affliction; even untimely death shall be entirely avoided. Furthermore, no harm shall come from any poisonous drugs, malevolent spirits, curses, or sorcery intended to injure others, nor from tigers, wolves, lions, venomous snakes, or even down to mosquitoes and gadflies. None of these shall cause them any injury.
The lower section consists of five vows.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion beginning with "We vow to sever... and so forth.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Excellent, excellent!"

These divine mantras all possess great power; they can fulfill whatever matters sentient beings seek according to their hearts' desires, providing great benefit, except in cases where there is a lack of sincere devotion.
"Do not harbor doubts," the Buddha said,
sealing his words with his seal.
When the great assembly had heard the Buddha’s words, they received them with joy and faith.
The fourth section of the lower grade:

Practice and Implementation. Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Great Goddess of Eloquence (Five Manuscripts). Chapter Fifteen, Part One: The Chapter on the Great Goddess of Eloquence. This chapter is analyzed according to three sections:
the intent of its inclusion, the explanation of its title, and the resolution of difficulties.
Regarding the intent of this discourse, there are three parts within the *Pravartana* (Circulation) section. First is the circulation through practice.
Within that, it further states: "The following five chapters constitute the third [section], which causes merit and wisdom to increase."
Within the increase of merit and wisdom, there are four aspects:
first, the increase of eloquence; second, the increase of clothing; third, the increase of food and drink; and fourth, the increase of wisdom.
For what reason is this so?
If one wishes to circulate the Dharma to benefit others, one must rely upon eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to provide explanations;
yet, even if one possesses wondrous eloquence, if one lacks clothing, one’s appearance will not be dignified.
Just as the four great elements become depleted and exhausted when deprived of food and drink,
there is also the fear that one will be unable to endure the suffering of scarcity and thus regress from practicing the two benefits.
Even if one were able to practice them, there is the fear that one might act out of a sense of dread or seeking, speaking with a defiled mind.
Therefore, one increases food and drink so as to eliminate such conditions.

Even if one possesses the necessary resources, if one lacks wisdom, one cannot comprehend the conventional and ultimate truths; because one would then explain the Dharma erroneously, one must increase wisdom.

Regarding the two types of beneficial practice, the benefit of others takes precedence; since the teaching of the Dharma to benefit sentient beings necessarily relies upon the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledges are explained first, and thus this chapter arises.
As for the explanation of the title: in Sanskrit it is called *Mahāsarvajñāpāṭī*, which in Chinese means "Great All-Knowing Eloquence"; *Devaputrī* means "Heavenly Maiden."
First, the general explanation of the great meaning is briefly fourfold, as stated in the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*: "Furthermore, there are four kinds of greatness:
first, the greatness of transcendence, because it transcends the three realms of existence and the five destinies."
Second is the greatness of tranquility, because it tends toward non-abiding nirvana.
Third is the greatness of merit, because the two accumulations of merit and wisdom increase.
Fourth is the greatness of benefiting beings, because one constantly relies on great compassion and does not abandon sentient beings.

"Pratibhāna" (eloquence) refers to the four types of eloquence; "pratibhāna" is swift wisdom (*jñāna*), and "prati" refers to skill (*kauśalya*). Because one possesses swift wisdom and skill, it is called "pratibhāna.
Since this pratibhāna is subsumed by the four kinds of greatness (*mahattva*), it is termed "Great Eloquence" (*mahā-pratibhāna*).
The gods are called "heavenly" (*deva*) because they employ sovereign power and possess radiant purity; they are also the "Heaven of Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha-deva*).
These gods possess great eloquence (*mahā-pratibhāna*), and since this Great Eloquence Heaven is female, she is called the "Goddess of Great Eloquence" (*Mahāpratisarā-devī*).
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"Because the Bodhisattva of this ninth stage possesses the four types of analytical eloquence (pratisaṃvid) and is further able to bestow them upon others, this title is established.
Regarding the threefold resolution of difficulties, the question is:
Among the four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), which one is this?
Answer: There are four in total.
How is this known? The text below states:
"Possessing the eloquence of fully adorned speech," which refers to the unimpeded eloquence of words (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
"Regarding the letters, phrases, and meanings within this sutra" refers to the two types of eloquence: that of phenomena (*dharma*) and that of meaning (*artha*).
The essence of a sūtra has two aspects: first, the expressive text; second, the expressed meaning. Both are termed "sūtra.

"Skillfully awakening others" refers to the unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); thus, it is summarized as "furthermore possessing *dhāraṇī*, total retention, and unimpededness. Here, *dhāraṇī* refers to the four types of retention, while "unimpededness" refers to the four types of unimpeded eloquence that are retained.
Question:
What is the difference between the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the four unhindered eloquences (*pratibhāna*)? Answer:
To comprehend the four [unhindered knowledges] without obstruction is called "understanding" (*prativedha*); to explain the four without obstruction is called "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
Eloquence arises based on understanding, while understanding is manifested through eloquence, for their essence is wisdom (*prajñā*).
In various sūtras and śāstras, these may be treated in relation to one another, yet they are often spoken of collectively as the "four."
Holding the four types of non-forgetfulness is called the four *dhāraṇīs*, which comprise both mindfulness and wisdom.
Question:
Now that this goddess possesses such thorough mastery of the *dhāraṇīs*, why is she not named the Goddess of the Great *Dhāraṇī*?
Answer:
The dhāraṇī is the cause, and the four dharmas it upholds are the fruit; thus, it is designated by its preeminent fruit rather than by the name of its cause.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Discernment (pratibhāna) is for the benefit of others, whereas retention (dhāraṇī) is superior for one's own benefit;
therefore, it is called "great discernment" because it excels that of others. Thus, below, Cunda requests: "May the goddess of wisdom and discernment bestow upon all excellent speech."

The invocation within the *Hīnayāna-śikṣā-saṃgraha* also states: "I pay homage to Sarasvatī, that my speech may be unimpeded," and so forth; in reality, this is a prayer for her to bestow all [blessings].
Sūtra. At that time, the Goddess Mahāpratisarā rose from her seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Commentary states: Regarding the text of this chapter, it is divided into three major sections:

first, the designation of the benefits and the accomplishment of capability; second, from "World-Honored One, I shall... onwards, the demonstration of the method for seeking [the path]; and third, from "At that time, the Buddha told... onwards, the World-Honored One’s praise and exhortation.
Within the first section, there are again two parts:
first, the ritual for requesting the teaching; second, the benefit for the practitioner.
This is the former.
In the Sūtra, from the passage "If there be a Dharma Master who preaches this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*," the second section has two parts:
first, benefiting the person who upholds and preaches it; second, from "Furthermore, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*" onwards, benefiting those who hear and study it.
This first [category] further has two parts:
first, those who should be benefited.
The Sūtra says: "I shall augment their wisdom and provide them with the eloquence of fully adorned speech."
Regarding the two lower categories of the dharmas that benefit others, there are three parts:
first, a general heading; second, a specific enumeration beginning with "Endowed with"; and third, a conclusion stating "Mastering the unimpeded."

Within the section on distinctions, the first part concerns the unimpeded eloquence of dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); the second part, beginning with "If that Dharma-master," concerns other forms of eloquence and dhāraṇīs.
This constitutes both the general heading and the specific details regarding the unimpeded eloquence of dharma.
On these nine stages, one attains the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), because among the eighteen transformations, one bestows eloquence upon others.
What is meant by "fully adorned" refers to the eight qualities of speech and so forth.

Sūtra: "If that Dharma master should forget any of the words, phrases, or meanings within this sūtra, [the Buddha] shall cause him to remember and uphold them all, enabling him to achieve skillful awakening; furthermore, he shall be granted the dhāraṇī of total retention free from obstruction."
The second section below, "Distinguishing from Other Eloquences," concerns the words and phrases, which are the Dharma.
Here, "wen" (ornament/phrase) is identical to "zi" (character/syllable);
thus, essence and function are explained together. This is the basis for that which expresses, yet its essence is not itself the expresser.
Phrases (*pada*) are that which can express; they express various meanings, though here "name" (*nāman*) is omitted for brevity.

To cause [the practitioner] to remember and maintain them all constitutes the retention of phenomena and their meaning (*dharmārthadhāraṇī*). Since the words and their meanings are what is maintained, that which is capable of remembering and maintaining them is the *dhāraṇī*; this is a statement that combines both cause and effect.
"Being able to skillfully awaken others" refers to the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
"Furthermore, together with *dhāraṇī*" refers to the two types of *dhāraṇī*: mantra and patience (*kṣānti*).
"Mastering *dhāraṇī* without obstruction" is the conclusion.

Sūtra: "Furthermore, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, for those sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and are destined to uphold it, shall be widely circulated throughout Jambudvīpa and shall not quickly disappear."
The second section clarifies the benefit for those who hear and study [the teaching].
This is divided into two parts:

first, it explains how the Dharma will long endure for those who should practice it; second, from the phrase "furthermore, it causes" onwards, it explains how it enables students to attain great benefit.
The initial passage has two parts:
first, clarifying the purpose;

second, [the fact that] the Dharma has long circulated, which is the same as in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "If one can give rise to a single thought of pure faith, know that they have already made offerings to many Buddhas."

The Sūtra states: “Furthermore, it causes immeasurable sentient beings who hear this sutra to all attain inconceivable, swift, and sharp eloquence, as well as inexhaustible great wisdom, and to become skillfully proficient in various treatises and technical arts.”
There are three benefits gained from the preliminary study:
first, the attainment of eloquence in the present; second, the future realization of the fruit of Buddhahood; and third, the increase of lifespan and so forth in the present.
Regarding the attainment of eloquence, one first acquires swift and sharp eloquence, namely, the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*) and the eloquence of words (*pada*).
The ability to manifest all sounds in a single kṣaṇa is called "quickness and sharpness" (*jāghanya*).
Within eloquent speech (*pratibhāna*), there are further seven types:
first, "rapid eloquence," because it flows like a cascading river in continuous succession without delay or hesitation.
Second is swift eloquence (*javanapratibhāna*), because one speaks immediately upon being prompted without stammering;
third is appropriate eloquence (*yuktapratibhāna*), because it accords with the occasion;
fourth is unerring eloquence (*avyavakīrṇapratibhāna*), because what is spoken is correct.
Fifth is the eloquence that is uninterrupted, for it is like an unbroken chain;
sixth is the eloquence of abundant meaning and flavor, for it is sufficient in its principles and reasoning;
seventh is the most supreme and wondrous eloquence, for nothing in the world surpasses it.
"Quickness" (*jaitri*) refers to the first two types of eloquence; "inexhaustibility" (*akṣaya*) refers to the fifth; "great wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) refers to the remaining ones.
"Skillfully understanding various treatises," and so forth, refers to the eloquence of Dharma and meaning (*dharmārtha-pratibhāna*).
"Inconceivable" refers to that which encompasses the four propositions.
Its wondrous functioning cannot be fathomed; thus it is called "inconceivable.
The Sūtra states: "One is able to transcend birth and death and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Below, one shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
Scripture: "In this present life, one's lifespan is increased, and all requisites for sustaining the body are made fully complete.
Below, this refers to the subsequent increase of the present lifespan and so forth.
Sūtra: “World-Honored One!

I shall, for the sake of those Dharma-preachers who uphold this sūtra and other sentient beings who delight in hearing this scripture, explain the method of bathing with incantations and medicinal herbs.”
The commentary states:
The following section shows the method for seeking [eloquence] and has two parts:

first, showing the maintenance of the sutra and the seeking of the skillful means for discernment; second, from "At that time, the Dharma-preacher receives a prediction," onwards, it is the actual seeking of eloquence.
The first section has four parts:
